The HAQ is a valid measure of disability, but is too insensitive to detect small but significant changes in disability.
the HAQ score changes for 207 clinic RA patients over a year showed no significant association with the patients' reported health status.

the minimum size of HAQ score change that can be confidently considered to reflect a clinically significant change in disability for individual patients with RA is 0.31 points or more, and that HAQ score changes less than this are unlikely to reflect significant changes to disability.

the development of a new instrument, the Health Assessment Questionnaire, to be used in the assessment of patients with arthritis.
the question of whether the HAQ has any use as an outcome measure for the individual patient.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the HAQ is a useful tool for monitoring the overall health of groups of patients with RA but is not a useful tool for individual patient monitoring of health status.
the HAQ score has no place in clinical monitoring.
HAQ score change is a useful group outcome measure but is not a reliable individual patient outcome measure.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Stanford HAQ has limited utility as a monitoring tool, but is a useful tool for assessing the severity of RA at a single point in time.
the HAQ is not a good monitoring tool for subjects in the clinic setting.
the Stanford Health Assessment questionnaire has potential as a monitoring and outcome tool for patients with RA.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the HAQ score is a good measure of disability in the aggregate.
it is not possible to reliably interpret HAQ score changes as reflecting a change in health for the individual patient.
it is not possible to determine whether the HAQ has changed in a clinically significant way from one assessment to the next in an individual patient.
